reconcile.connective: Commentators uniformly read Luke's "hate" as a Semitic idiom of comparison — "love less" — so it sets priority, not literal enmity, and never cancels the command to love.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells, compiler of the Skeptic's Annotated Bible, presses Luke 14:26 as a blunt clash with the love commands, calling the demand to hate one's family cruel and "against family values."

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (2013)

excerpts.excerpt_text: And hate not — Matthew, Mat 10:37, expresses the true meaning of this word, when he says, He who loveth his father and mother More than me. … and that this is no arbitrary interpretation of the word hate, but one agreeable to the Hebrew idiom, appears from what is said on Gen 29:30, Gen 29:31, where Leah's being hated is explained by Rachel's being loved more than Leah.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly addresses the love/hate tension: argues 'hate' in Luke 14:26 is the Hebrew idiom for 'love less,' citing Matthew's parallel and Leah/Rachel — the core harmonization.

excerpts.excerpt_text: not that proper hatred of any, or all of these, is enjoined by Christ; for this would be contrary to the laws of God, to the first principles of nature, to all humanity, to the light of nature, to reason and divine revelation: but that these are not to be preferred to Christ, or loved more than he, as it is explained in Mat 10:37
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Explicitly denies that literal hatred is commanded — would contradict God's law — and recasts 'hate' as not preferring family above Christ, dissolving the conflict with the love commands.

excerpts.excerpt_text: The phrase by comparison does not appear in the Greek, but it accurately represents Jesus' meaning. Love for family and one's own life must not compete with devotion to Christ.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: A concise distinct voice confirming the comparative reading: 'hate' = relative priority of Christ over family, not literal hatred, so the love commands stand.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), note on Luke 14:26
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke treats this exact passage, arguing 'hate' renders the Hebrew idiom for 'love less' (Matthew 10:37; Genesis 29:30-31), so Luke 14:26 sets priority rather than commanding literal hatred.
